concepts.def: A clear, testable statement predicting an outcome, which a practical food investigation is designed to support or reject through evidence.
A structured method of judging food using the senses, often with tasting panels and rating or ranking tests to compare products objectively.
An investigation in which only one variable is changed while all other conditions are kept the same, so results can be reliably compared.
A condition, such as oven temperature or cooking time, kept constant during an experiment so it does not distort the comparison being made.
A spider-diagram chart used in sensory analysis to plot scores for attributes such as taste, texture, colour and aroma of a food product.
The stage of a research project where results are analysed against the original aim, conclusions are drawn and improvements are suggested.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Research Project / Practical Food Studies — a core area of A-Level Food Technology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Research Project / Practical Food Studies brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Research Project / Practical Food Studies.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In a fair test comparing two recipes, you should change:
options: Only one variable at a time
Every variable at once
No variables at all
The testers each time

mcqs.q: A spider diagram showing scores for taste, texture and aroma is called a:
options: Star profile
Bar chart
Pie chart
Flow chart

mcqs.q: A clear, testable prediction that an investigation sets out to examine is a:
options: Hypothesis
Conclusion
Control
Variable

mcqs.q: Using a tasting panel with ranking tests to compare products is an example of:
options: Sensory evaluation
Nutritional analysis
Cost analysis
Risk assessment

mcqs.q: In a fair test, how many variables should you change at once?
options: To increase the cost of the project.
As many as possible to get faster results.
Only one, so any difference in results can be linked to that change.
None, because variables should never change.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of a control in a food investigation?
options: To increase the cost of the project.
To make the experiment more complicated.
Sensory testing measures the calories in food.
To provide a standard, unchanged sample to compare the test results against.

mcqs.q: Does sensory testing give purely objective results?
options: Sensory scores are completely objective like a thermometer reading.
To increase the cost of the project.
Sensory testing measures the calories in food.
It is made more reliable with panels and structured tests, but tasting still involves personal judgement.

free_texts.q: What is the term for a step where control is essential to ensure food safety?
free_texts.hint: Three-word HACCP term, often abbreviated CCP.

sequence.def: Identify potential hazards in the process
Find critical control points where hazards are controlled
Check each control point during production
Act when a critical limit is breached
Confirm the system works and keep records
